detail.longDescription: The development of machine proof technology is indebted to the joint efforts of mathematicians and engineers over decades. Owing to the scalability of machine computation, it has become difficult for humans to fully verify the output of artificial intelligence. Formal verifiers taking part in the loop of artificial intelligence have gained recognition from mathematicians and others, and are currently a key node with the greatest promise for governing AI through AI. Several mathematicians have criticized some large companies for using AI in mathematical research without standards, in violation of the values of academic research. 17.3 million lines of Lean code were disclosed by a mathematics researcher at an AI company. This includes about 170,000 modules. The proof claims to already be a proof of the Riemann conjecture. As of the second day after its release, no professional mathematician had yet fully and completely and conclusively completed an evaluation of these proofs. Machine proof requires first describing the problem correctly, and then giving a proof within the language of machine proof. If the description of the problem is incorrect, or if incorrect and untenable "theorems" are introduced, compilation will pass while the proof does not hold. There may also be problems such as errors in the kernel of the prover, which the community has already reported. Lean also acknowledges the possibility of various errors. Yet Lean still claimed to "certify" the code in less than two days after the release of these 17.3 million lines. Lean still chooses to conflate formal compilation passing and checker results with proof in the strict mathematical sense. Lean does not take its own proof of a theorem as large as the Riemann conjecture seriously. It disregards the attitude of mathematicians and potential errors, and unilaterally claims "certify" for the result in language that sidesteps mathematical rigor. We cannot maliciously speculate that this is directly related to its being a product developed by the research institute of a technology company, but this is clearly not a sufficiently responsible way to treat mathematics, human society, and the development and governance of artificial intelligence. After the two World Wars, mathematicians became an important means for many people to plunder reputation and seek private gain. Some closed practices have also left the public dissatisfied; some people evade the responsibilities of researchers, exaggerate themselves as "the most intelligent class," and hold a hostile attitude toward social development, human society, the popularization of science, and the public's right to participate in mathematics and science. There is nothing noble in this. But we still believe that the rigorous methods of mathematics have a unique value — we do not have to live in a false world. Lean has betrayed the truth. Judging by the results, we do not yet know whether these 17.3 million lines of code actually have mathematical defects, nor do we know whether the versions by human mathematicians without artificial intelligence are necessarily free of defects; but judging by the process, Lean's current selective "certify" is irresponsible. Lean should be ashamed!
